Sequence 8 incorporates those into Understand. Sequence 13 separates plan preference from provision and challenges incomplete concealment. No participant observations, approvals, demonstrated proficiency or field results exist. Modeling does not satisfy the pending Understand review gate.

PURPOSE AND BOUNDARY
Model how an adult might choose an acceptable next action for the invented Community Drawing Hour while retaining control and manageable effort. The fictional notice offers morning or afternoon attendance and an unexplained instruction, “confirm your place.” The candidate cannot register anyone, establish real routes, reserve assistance or resolve that instruction through invented advice. Supported choice may include no action.

DEPENDENCY MODEL
A desired action depends on an opportunity: comprehensible service information, a usable route, suitable device conditions and assistance when wanted. These conditions are unknown. Service owners control notices and routes; library staff define assistance boundaries; device operators influence session behavior. None of their participation or resources is presumed. Investigate these conditions before attributing difficulty to patron learning.

STATE MODEL
Maintain independent fields:
Preference: online / check paper / check staffed help / unknown / none works / undecided.
Provision: unknown throughout this rehearsal; selections never confirm availability.
Next action: examine the notice / ask what “confirm” means if help exists / check another route / undecided / another optional fictional action.
Session visibility: visible / concealed. Content presence: draft present / cleared or lost. Activity: active / paused / stopped. Interruption is an event, not evidence of abandonment or completion.

REVIEWABLE TRANSITIONS
Choosing or correcting changes only explicit draft choices and their description. Confusion offers keep, revise, leave undecided or stop; it provides no unverified registration procedure. An interruption offers the same control plus conceal or clear, without requiring staff or automatic resumption. If content is lost, disclose the loss and offer a fresh undecided draft or stopping; never reconstruct an inferred plan.
Stopping ends the exercise without a completion judgment. While content remains, conceal and clear stay accessible. Conceal hides choices, optional notes and every derived summary together; the remaining view states that fictional content remains in the session. Explicit reveal restores visibility. Clear removes candidate-held choices, notes and summaries and visibly confirms its scope. It cannot promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Clearing while stopped must not restart the exercise.

ADOPTED MODEL REVISION
Sequence 13's challenge changes the privacy requirement from hiding notes to hiding all plan-bearing displays. Review must also examine feedback, interruption messages and reveal behavior. This is a meaningful requirement revision, with technical verification pending; it does not require rewriting the earlier problem frame.

LEARNING HYPOTHESIS AND FEEDBACK
A possible learning mechanism is practicing how to identify ambiguity, check an opportunity, seek help and change direction. Optional descriptive feedback could make an explicit choice easier to reconsider; effectiveness is unknown. Example: “Your draft selects checking for paper registration. Its availability is unknown. You may change, leave undecided or stop.” Do not infer skill, consent, readiness or transfer. No compulsory writing, explanation or reflection is required. Later adaptation would need a different fictional task and separate evidence, including whether support was still needed.

NON-AI AND SERVICE OPTIONS
Prepare a paper card with the same uncertainty, next-action, revision and stop choices. An ordinary conversation with available staff is another option. Examine readable wording, physical access and discreet paper handling. Also investigate clearer notices and verified route information; improving a service may remove the need for a planning tool. Review may favor an alternative or reject all candidates.

EVIDENCE AND HUMAN GATES — PENDING
Proposed comparison questions: Can reviewers find an acceptable action, including stopping? Do labels imply provision? What reading, privacy and assistance burdens arise? Can fictional content be corrected, concealed completely and cleared after interruption? Retain contrary accounts and distinguish task familiarity, reviewer prompting and service barriers from any learning explanation. Completion and speed are insufficient evidence.
Unknowns include route existence, staffing windows, language arrangements, accessibility needs, shared-device behavior and demand for this tool. Accountable patron and librarian review must address framing, privacy, access and workload before approved design or a pilot. Subsequent technical checks and human interaction testing remain required. No recruitment, review, launch or efficacy is asserted.

NEXT ACTION
Use this model to prepare a small screen outline, matching paper card and dependency questions sheet for review. Sequence 6 challenges the assumption that three offered routes constitute meaningful choice. The seed supplies the fictional task and restrictions. No participant observations, human approvals or field results exist.

PROBLEM FRAME
Investigate what enables adults to choose an acceptable next action for an unfamiliar service while retaining control, privacy and manageable effort. Barriers may lie in service design, available support, language or device access. Independent online completion is not the objective. A reasonable outcome can be seeking help, checking availability, leaving a plan undecided or stopping.

ADOPTED REVISION
The draft interaction must include “availability unknown,” “none works for me,” and “pause or stop,” without requiring a reason. Next actions may be selected, spoken, written or undecided. This changes both the interaction and its review criteria: a finished plan is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of supported choice. These are working requirements awaiting human review, not approved commitments.

FICTIONAL REVIEW MATERIAL
Exercise text: “Imagine a made-up library event called Community Drawing Hour. Its example notice offers morning or afternoon attendance and says ‘confirm your place’ without explaining how. This exercise cannot register anyone. Online, paper and staffed routes are possibilities to examine; their real availability is unknown.”

Planning card, usable on paper or as a later screen outline:
• Approach: online / check for paper / check for staffed help / availability unknown / none works / pause or stop.
• Next action: examine the fictional notice / ask what ‘confirm’ means if help is available / check whether another route exists / leave undecided / stop. A different fictional action may be expressed, but writing is optional.
• Change prompt: “The shared computer session ends before you continue, or the instruction remains confusing. Keep, change or abandon your plan.” Do not require recovery or an explanation.
• Feedback example: “Your draft selects checking for paper registration. Its availability remains unknown. You can change or stop this plan.” Feedback describes explicit choices only; it cannot establish access, readiness, consent, skill or transfer.

PRIVACY AND ACCESS BOUNDARIES
Use no real passwords, identifiers, contact details, account information or service records. Concealment must explain that fictional notes remain in the current session. Clearing must remove candidate-held notes and visibly confirm removal; it must not promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Examine what appears after interruption and session ending. Wording, languages, keyboard access and other participation arrangements require review. Can they revise, conceal, clear and stop with understandable consequences? What reading, privacy and assistance burdens does each approach introduce? Use fictional content only and retain contrary accounts. Difficulty could reflect instructions or unavailable opportunities; apparent ease could reflect prior familiarity. Later transfer would need separate evidence in another fictional task and cannot be inferred from completion here.

NEXT ACTION AND HUMAN GATE

Then arrange patron and librarian review of the problem framing, refusal paths, access arrangements, privacy wording and workload boundaries. response.artifact_body:
## Problem and people

Human-centered designer draft for public deliberation in a rehearsal. No patron, librarian, volunteer or practitioner has participated, approved these requirements or demonstrated their effectiveness. Sequence 2 preserves parent Understand, Map and Design context. Its embedded historical sequence labels are not additional evidence references. Sequences 5 and 7 supply the current domain and systems proposals.

The task is to explore the invented Community Drawing Hour, inspect an authored confirmation requirement and choose an acceptable next step. Relevant people include adult patrons with varied reading, language and device access; people providing assistance; and owners of service requirements. Participation may end with a choice, an unresolved condition, paper practice, passing or declining.

The discipline-specific challenge is that offering valid choices does not establish that people can understand, compare or exercise them with acceptable effort. A route board, support selector, initial snapshot, changed condition and final comparison could become a demanding exercise. A complete plan must not become the implied price of participation.

## Human and system capability

Human requirements: patrons retain authority over whether to participate, what help they want and which explanation represents their choice. Selecting, pointing or speaking may express a choice; silence must not be interpreted as agreement. Passing requires no reason. An actually available facilitator may read authored information or restate selections, but must accept correction and avoid steering toward a preferred route.

Librarians and service owners must establish real routes, assistance boundaries and feasible support arrangements before operational use. Affected-person and accessibility-practitioner review must determine whether this task is wanted, its wording is understandable and its privacy controls are usable. These human gates remain unmet.

System requirements: present the mission and route choices with text alternatives, keep fictional conditions distinct from unknown real provision, and reveal detail without forcing additional decisions. Generate descriptions only from explicit selections. No personal fields, account controls, scoring, inferred understanding, storage, network activity or automatic service requests are permitted.

A patron controls continuing and changing a preference. Service owners control actual participation requirements. Assistance providers control what support they offer. Choosing help cannot change its availability. These authority boundaries must appear where the dependent decision occurs, not solely in Help.

## Experience and decisions

Opening mission: “Community Drawing Hour is invented. Explore its example notice and choose a possible next step. This exercise cannot register anyone. Use fictional choices only.” The notice offers morning and afternoon sessions and says “Confirm your place.” Session preference is optional and must not resemble a reservation.

Use a small illustrated board with text labels: Explore the event, Choose a route, Check a condition, Review your plan. Illustrations provide orientation only. Do not require interaction with an illustration or completion of every step. Paper materials, Help, passing and stopping remain available from the opening.

The route decision offers mock online practice, staff explanation, paper practice and pause or decline, with equally reachable “No route works for me” and “Leave undecided.” No route is preselected. Selecting a route reveals one short consequence and its condition; it does not advance automatically. Longer explanation is available through “More detail,” which can be closed without changing choices or losing focus.

For online practice, show “This invented portal includes an account step. No account is created here.” Controls inspect the requirement, reconsider the route or stop; there are no account or contact fields. Staff explanation records a desired explanation and states that real assistance and language support are unknown. Paper practice opens complete fictional materials and states that real paper acceptance is unknown.

The patron may optionally keep the current selection as an initial plan. Skipping this leaves “Initial plan not recorded.” It does not block the changed condition, current plan or paper route. Support choices are optional and unselected by default; “None selected” does not mean no support is needed.

Offer the authored change: “Imagine staff are temporarily unavailable during this fictional visit.” Applying it preserves the selected route and marks its assistance dependency unresolved. Show options to keep the preference, reconsider, wait without a promised duration, leave undecided, pause or stop. Do not substitute an online route.

Review shows initial and current route, next action, support preference, control boundary and fallback using short labelled lines. “Fictional plan; no registration or request sent” remains adjacent to the output. “Correct initial plan” and “Change current plan” identify the side being edited. Cancellation preserves both sides. No reason for correction is requested.

Optional Neighborhood Story Circle practice uses fewer suggestions, but retains Help, paper, passing and correction. Choosing it clearly explains that it replaces the current task and offers cancellation. Requesting more support has no penalty and produces no capability label.

## Requirements and rationale

R1 — Limit entry burden. Origin: Human-centered designer, D2.prototyping and D5.context; route journey at sequence 5 and bounded comparison at sequence 7. Make the core task one route choice followed by inspection of its consequence. Session, support, initial snapshot and changed-condition practice remain optional. This supports participation without demanding a full planning worksheet. Acceptance check: a reviewer can inspect an online requirement and leave with an undecided next action without completing other selectors; no blocked control, missing-field message or completion judgment appears. Uncertainty: acceptable reading and interaction effort has not been established with patrons.

R2 — Preserve choice without steering. Origin: Human-centered designer, D3.agency; meaningful refusal at sequences 2 and 5. Put passing, undecided and no workable route alongside the decision, with comparable visual weight and neutral wording. Include “My next action is not listed” without requiring free text. Selecting it yields an unresolved description, not an inferred answer. Acceptance check: exercise each refusal path and inspect the output for unchanged authority, no justification prompt and no deficit label. Uncertainty: visible refusal may still feel socially difficult in facilitated use; affected-person review is required.

R3 — Keep dependency information local. Origin: Human-centered designer, D3.agency and D5.context; preference/provision separation at sequences 5 and 7. Show the fictional requirement, unknown real availability and controlling party near each route consequence. Keep these statements visible when longer detail is collapsed. Acceptance check: select staff explanation, apply fictional unavailability and close detail; preference remains visible, availability is unresolved and no staff request or assistance is confirmed. Context: this is an authored change, not an observed service incident.

R4 — Make representation correctable. Origin: Human-centered designer, D2.prototyping and D3.agency; snapshot rules at sequence 7. Use plain labels for initial and current plans, with distinct correction controls. Feedback describes only the changed selection and its dependency. Correction must replace dependent descriptions without retaining obsolete claims elsewhere. Acceptance check: record staff explanation, change the current route to paper, correct the initial route to undecided and cancel another edit. Both sides and all feedback must reflect precisely those explicit actions. Uncertainty: comprehension of two-plan comparison is untested; review may remove it while retaining a correctable current plan.

R5 — Support access without promising provision. Origin: Human-centered designer, D5.context; language and facilitation concerns at sequence 5. Use short text labels, meaningful text alternatives, visible keyboard focus and responsive reflow. Detail expansion returns focus to its trigger when closed; changing a selection must not move focus unexpectedly. Oral assistance is conditional on an available person. Language support remains unknown. Acceptance check: inspect the journey using keyboard operation, narrow layout, magnification and assistive technology; verify route labels, consequences and refusal remain reachable without illustration interpretation. These are proposed technical checks, not an accessibility certification. Patron review must determine wording and language arrangements.

R6 — Preserve privacy and stopping throughout. Origin: Human-centered designer, D2.prototyping and D3.agency; parent controls preserved at sequence 2 and state separation at sequence 7. Place Cover, Clear and Stop before task controls in keyboard order. Cover removes every choice-bearing view from visual, keyboard and assistive-technology access and moves focus to neutral status. Reveal restores visibility only; paused or stopped activity requires explicit resumption. A clear confirmation must remain usable while covered and must not expose choices. Confirmed clearing removes initial/current plans and all derived messages, preserves paused or stopped activity and reports its limited scope. Cancellation preserves content. Acceptance check: exercise cover, reveal, cancel, confirmed clear and resume from comparison and optional-practice states; inspect focus and stale content. No check has been executed, and device-wide deletion cannot be claimed.

R7 — Keep practice and support voluntary. Origin: Human-centered designer, D3.agency and D5.context; optional second task at sequences 5 and 7. Practice unlocks nothing. Fewer suggestions must not remove Help or make support harder to request. A facilitator reads or restates only with permission and never treats silence as agreement. Acceptance check: skip practice, enter it, request detail, cancel replacement and stop; no reward, score or assertion of independence appears. Human review must examine prompting and facilitation effort. Learning or transfer cannot be inferred from these interactions.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

Progressive detail reduces initial reading but can obscure conditions; therefore essential fiction, availability and control statements remain visible beside decisions. A before/after view makes changes inspectable but adds memory demands; it is optional and may be removed after review. Fixed choices limit personal-data solicitation but can miss an acceptable action; unlisted and undecided outcomes must remain valid.

Retain dissent that improving the service notice or removing an unnecessary account step could address the barrier more directly. Ordinary conversation with available staff and the complete paper packet below are non-AI options. Reviewers may choose an alternative or reject the candidate.

Complete invented paper/facilitation packet:

Card A — Mission and notice. “Community Drawing Hour is fictional. Its notice offers morning and afternoon sessions and says ‘Confirm your place.’ Explore a possible next step. This does not register anyone. Use no personal information. Point, speak, mark, pass, pause or stop.” Session preference may be left blank.

Card B — Routes and consequences. “Online practice: inspect an invented account step; create no account and provide no details. Staff explanation: seek an explanation if suitable assistance exists; real availability and language support are unknown. Paper practice: use these cards; real service acceptance of paper is unknown. You may choose no workable route, remain undecided, pause or decline.”

Card C — Optional initial plan. “Route: online practice / staff explanation / paper practice / no workable route / undecided. Next action: inspect requirement / seek explanation if assistance exists / examine another route / wait without a promised duration / my action is not listed / undecided / pause / stop. Support wanted: explanation / reading aloud / language assistance / device assistance / none selected. Fallback: another route / remain undecided / pause / stop.” Leave any item blank. No explanation is required.

Card D — Changed condition. “Imagine staff are temporarily unavailable during this fictional visit. Your preferred route can stay the same while assistance is unresolved. Keep, change, wait without a promised duration, leave undecided, pause or stop. No alternative becomes available because you select it.”

Card E — Current plan and correction. Repeat Card C’s choices for the current plan. “You control continuing. The service owner controls the event requirement. Assistance providers control offered support. Fictional plan; no registration or request sent.” Identify whether a correction changes the initial or current plan. Replace a mark or ask for a restatement; a reason is unnecessary. An unrecorded initial plan stays unrecorded.

Card F — Handling and facilitation. “Before marking, agree how cards will be handled. Folding or covering conceals them; it does not erase them. Leave cards unmarked if preferred.” Facilitator script: “Would you like to point, speak, mark, pass or stop? Shall I read the notice? Which route, if any? Would you like the imagined change? Shall I restate your choice so you can correct it?” Wait for an explicit response; do not select an answer, promise assistance, collect personal information or infer understanding. Facilitation requires an actually available person.

Optional practice card — “Neighborhood Story Circle is invented. Its notice says ‘Check joining arrangements.’ Choose a route and next action using Cards B and C. Imagine your shared-computer time ends. Keep, change, pause or stop. Review using Card E.” Further explanation is available on request, without penalty. This exercise establishes no learning or transfer.

## Acceptance checks

Intended quality is a manageable, correctable decision that preserves participation authority and makes dependencies understandable. Requirements R1–R7 specify proposed observable checks; none has been performed. Intended quality must remain separate from observed technical behavior, which is currently absent.

Technical verification should inspect all reachable states for keyboard focus, text alternatives, reflow, cancellation, complete concealment, faithful summaries and confirmed clearing. It must also verify absence of network, storage, telemetry, personal fields and external navigation.

Affected-person and practitioner review must separately examine whether the task is wanted, whether refusal feels legitimate, which explanations are misunderstood and who bears reading or facilitation work. Do not treat speed, completion, a route change or reduced prompting as evidence of learning, transfer or flourishing.

## Evidence and unknowns

Sequence 2 is preserved context, not a reported interruption or newly verified finding. Sequence 5 is a domain draft; sequence 7 is a systems draft. Neither supplies human approval or executed checks. Field evidence remains pending.

What changes after the hypothetical unavailable-staff challenge: the assistance dependency becomes unresolved while the preference remains under patron control. This contribution additionally makes the initial snapshot optional, keeps critical conditions visible in collapsed views and preserves help during less-prompted practice. These refine current Design; no earlier artifact revision is requested.

Rival explanations for difficulty include unfamiliar wording, language mismatch, inaccessible controls, unnecessary service requirements, limited device time and missing assistance. Apparent ease could reflect prior familiarity or facilitator steering. Unknowns include demand for the exercise, real route availability, paper acceptance, language arrangements, discoverable privacy controls and sustainable support workload.

Agency, dignity, access, belonging and workload require review of actual participation conditions. Learning and transfer require separate inquiry with support and prior familiarity documented. No outcome in these dimensions has been observed.

## Next decision

Prepare a compact screen outline and the complete paper packet for pending patron, librarian and accessibility-practitioner review. Compare whether people can inspect a condition and retain control with acceptable effort, including through paper or refusal. Retain dissent and corrections. A later Build may implement a candidate for technical and interaction testing; this draft supplies no approval, pilot authorization or efficacy claim.

response.challenged_assumption: A route board and correctable before/after plan inherently provide manageable, voluntary participation, and fewer prompts indicate greater independence.
response.decision: Refine current Design with optional comparison, locally visible dependencies and equivalent refusal and support paths; prepare paired screen and paper materials for pending human review.
drawbacks: Progressive detail can make important conditions harder to discover.
Fixed choices may omit a patron’s preferred next action.
Paper preparation, language review and facilitation add work.
flourishing: Agency and dignity include refusing the exercise without justification or an ability judgment.
Access and belonging depend on usable language, device and assistance conditions that remain unknown.
Sustainable workload, learning and transfer require separate reviewed evidence; a completed plan establishes none.
human_capabilities: Patrons control choosing, passing, correcting, pausing and declining through selection, pointing or speech.
Librarians and facilitators must assess support boundaries, handling effort and sustainable workload.
Affected people and accessibility practitioners must review comprehension, language access and shared-device use.
response.message: Sequence 2 preserves parent context; it supplies no new participant evidence, approval or technical finding. Sequences 5 and 7 establish useful route and recovery proposals. My Human-centered design challenge is that a visible route board and correctable comparison can still impose reading, memory and facilitation work, while making a finished plan feel expected. The Design should let people inspect one route, pass without explanation and request more detail without losing their place. Optional practice must retain access to support. These are draft requirements; affected-person and practitioner review remains pending.
objections: Clearer event notices or removal of an unnecessary account step may make the tool unnecessary.
A patron may prefer conversation, paper or stopping over an illustrated digital journey.
A library may lack capacity for facilitation, printing or reviewed language versions.
risks: A polished journey could imply real registration, available assistance or expected completion.
Facilitator prompting could substitute another person’s choice for the patron’s.
Reading difficulty or interrupted participation could be misclassified as a patron deficit.
system_capabilities: Present a short route decision with explicit fictional conditions and optional detail.
Keep support preferences separate from availability and generate faithful, correctable descriptions.
Provide keyboard access, text alternatives, cancellation, cover/resume and complete candidate-held clearing.
tradeoffs: Keep route conditions visible while revealing longer explanations on request.
Make comparison optional while preserving faithful correction of both plans.
Reduce suggestions in optional practice while keeping help equally reachable.

## Human and system capability

Human requirements: patrons retain authority over continuing and correcting their choices. Pointing, speaking, passing and declining remain legitimate. Available facilitators may read an authored notice or restate an explicit selection, but must not infer agreement, supply a preferred answer or promise assistance. Librarians and service owners must establish actual service conditions before any later operational use.

System requirements: distinguish the patron's preference, the fictional condition being explored, real provision that remains unknown, and the draft next action. Selecting staff help records a preference; it cannot create a staffed opportunity. Selecting paper practice opens complete invented materials; it cannot establish real paper acceptance. The mock online route may describe an account requirement but must contain no account or credential controls.

The coupling is conditional: a desired action may depend on understandable information, a usable route, device time and suitable assistance. The candidate can expose those dependencies and support reconsideration. It cannot supply missing service capacity. Authority over the event requirement belongs to the service owner; authority over offered assistance belongs to its provider; the patron controls participation in this exercise.

## Experience and decisions

Keep the primary journey short: explore the invented notice, choose a route, inspect one condition and review a draft. Use the four text-labelled route choices proposed in the seed: mock online practice, staff explanation, complete paper practice, and pause/decline. Also permit no workable route and undecided without requiring an explanation. Use fixed controls and no open-text fields for this candidate.

The first review describes the current choice. An optional explicit action, “Keep this as my initial plan,” records a temporary comparison snapshot. The current plan describes route, next action, control boundary, requested support and fallback. It always states “Fictional plan; no registration or request sent.” Changed fields receive descriptive feedback, such as “You changed from staff explanation to paper practice. Selecting a route must reveal its authored requirement, the party controlling it, real provision marked unknown and an action the patron can choose. The initial/current comparison makes a changed decision inspectable but adds state and wording. Keep it optional, retain only two temporary snapshots and show expanded explanations on request. Correctability matters more than filling every field.

Preserve dissent that a planning tool may be unnecessary. A clearer notice, verified route information or removal of a needless account step could address the barrier at its source. Complete paper practice and an ordinary conversation with available staff are non-AI options. None establishes operational service access.

Choosing help cannot change its availability. These authority boundaries must appear where the dependent decision occurs, not solely in Help.

## Experience and decisions

Opening mission: “Community Drawing Hour is invented. Explore its example notice and choose a possible next step. This exercise cannot register anyone. Use fictional choices only.” The notice offers morning and afternoon sessions and says “Confirm your place.” Session preference is optional and must not resemble a reservation.

Use a small illustrated board with text labels: Explore the event, Choose a route, Check a condition, Review your plan. Illustrations provide orientation only. Do not require interaction with an illustration or completion of every step. Paper materials, Help, passing and stopping remain available from the opening.

The route decision offers mock online practice, staff explanation, paper practice and pause or decline, with equally reachable “No route works for me” and “Leave undecided.” No route is preselected. Selecting a route reveals one short consequence and its condition; it does not advance automatically. Longer explanation is available through “More detail,” which can be closed without changing choices or losing focus.

For online practice, show “This invented portal includes an account step. No account is created here.” Controls inspect the requirement, reconsider the route or stop; there are no account or contact fields. Staff explanation records a desired explanation and states that real assistance and language support are unknown. Paper practice opens complete fictional materials and states that real paper acceptance is unknown.

The patron may optionally keep the current selection as an initial plan. Skipping this leaves “Initial plan not recorded.” It does not block the changed condition, current plan or paper route. Support choices are optional and unselected by default; “None selected” does not mean no support is needed.

Offer the authored change: “Imagine staff are temporarily unavailable during this fictional visit.” Applying it preserves the selected route and marks its assistance dependency unresolved. Show options to keep the preference, reconsider, wait without a promised duration, leave undecided, pause or stop. Do not substitute an online route.

Review shows initial and current route, next action, support preference, control boundary and fallback using short labelled lines. “Fictional plan; no registration or request sent” remains adjacent to the output. “Correct initial plan” and “Change current plan” identify the side being edited. Cancellation preserves both sides. No reason for correction is requested.

Optional Neighborhood Story Circle practice uses fewer suggestions, but retains Help, paper, passing and correction. Choosing it clearly explains that it replaces the current task and offers cancellation. Requesting more support has no penalty and produces no capability label.

## Requirements and rationale

R1 — Limit entry burden. Origin: Human-centered designer, D2.prototyping and D5.context; route journey at sequence 5 and bounded comparison at sequence 7. Make the core task one route choice followed by inspection of its consequence. Session, support, initial snapshot and changed-condition practice remain optional. This supports participation without demanding a full planning worksheet. Acceptance check: a reviewer can inspect an online requirement and leave with an undecided next action without completing other selectors; no blocked control, missing-field message or completion judgment appears. Uncertainty: acceptable reading and interaction effort has not been established with patrons.

R2 — Preserve choice without steering. Origin: Human-centered designer, D3.agency; meaningful refusal at sequences 2 and 5. Put passing, undecided and no workable route alongside the decision, with comparable visual weight and neutral wording. Include “My next action is not listed” without requiring free text. Selecting it yields an unresolved description, not an inferred answer. Acceptance check: exercise each refusal path and inspect the output for unchanged authority, no justification prompt and no deficit label. Uncertainty: visible refusal may still feel socially difficult in facilitated use; affected-person review is required.

R3 — Keep dependency information local. Origin: Human-centered designer, D3.agency and D5.context; preference/provision separation at sequences 5 and 7. Show the fictional requirement, unknown real availability and controlling party near each route consequence. Keep these statements visible when longer detail is collapsed. Acceptance check: select staff explanation, apply fictional unavailability and close detail; preference remains visible, availability is unresolved and no staff request or assistance is confirmed. Context: this is an authored change, not an observed service incident.

R4 — Make representation correctable. Origin: Human-centered designer, D2.prototyping and D3.agency; snapshot rules at sequence 7. Use plain labels for initial and current plans, with distinct correction controls. Feedback describes only the changed selection and its dependency. Correction must replace dependent descriptions without retaining obsolete claims elsewhere. Acceptance check: record staff explanation, change the current route to paper, correct the initial route to undecided and cancel another edit. Both sides and all feedback must reflect precisely those explicit actions. Uncertainty: comprehension of two-plan comparison is untested; review may remove it while retaining a correctable current plan.

R5 — Support access without promising provision. Origin: Human-centered designer, D5.context; language and facilitation concerns at sequence 5. Use short text labels, meaningful text alternatives, visible keyboard focus and responsive reflow. Detail expansion returns focus to its trigger when closed; changing a selection must not move focus unexpectedly. Oral assistance is conditional on an available person. Language support remains unknown. Acceptance check: inspect the journey using keyboard operation, narrow layout, magnification and assistive technology; verify route labels, consequences and refusal remain reachable without illustration interpretation. These are proposed technical checks, not an accessibility certification. Patron review must determine wording and language arrangements.

R6 — Preserve privacy and stopping throughout. Origin: Human-centered designer, D2.prototyping and D3.agency; parent controls preserved at sequence 2 and state separation at sequence 7. Place Cover, Clear and Stop before task controls in keyboard order. Cover removes every choice-bearing view from visual, keyboard and assistive-technology access and moves focus to neutral status. Reveal restores visibility only; paused or stopped activity requires explicit resumption. A clear confirmation must remain usable while covered and must not expose choices. Confirmed clearing removes initial/current plans and all derived messages, preserves paused or stopped activity and reports its limited scope. Cancellation preserves content. Acceptance check: exercise cover, reveal, cancel, confirmed clear and resume from comparison and optional-practice states; inspect focus and stale content. No check has been executed, and device-wide deletion cannot be claimed.

R7 — Keep practice and support voluntary. Origin: Human-centered designer, D3.agency and D5.context; optional second task at sequences 5 and 7. Practice unlocks nothing. Fewer suggestions must not remove Help or make support harder to request. A facilitator reads or restates only with permission and never treats silence as agreement. Acceptance check: skip practice, enter it, request detail, cancel replacement and stop; no reward, score or assertion of independence appears. Human review must examine prompting and facilitation effort. Learning or transfer cannot be inferred from these interactions.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

Progressive detail reduces initial reading but can obscure conditions; therefore essential fiction, availability and control statements remain visible beside decisions. A before/after view makes changes inspectable but adds memory demands; it is optional and may be removed after review. Fixed choices limit personal-data solicitation but can miss an acceptable action; unlisted and undecided outcomes must remain valid.

Retain dissent that improving the service notice or removing an unnecessary account step could address the barrier more directly. Ordinary conversation with available staff and the complete paper packet below are non-AI options. Reviewers may choose an alternative or reject the candidate.

Complete invented paper/facilitation packet:

Card A — Mission and notice. “Community Drawing Hour is fictional. Its notice offers morning and afternoon sessions and says ‘Confirm your place.’ Explore a possible next step. This does not register anyone. Use no personal information. Point, speak, mark, pass, pause or stop.” Session preference may be left blank.

Card B — Routes and consequences. “Online practice: inspect an invented account step; create no account and provide no details. Staff explanation: seek an explanation if suitable assistance exists; real availability and language support are unknown. Paper practice: use these cards; real service acceptance of paper is unknown. You may choose no workable route, remain undecided, pause or decline.”

Card C — Optional initial plan. “Route: online practice / staff explanation / paper practice / no workable route / undecided. Next action: inspect requirement / seek explanation if assistance exists / examine another route / wait without a promised duration / my action is not listed / undecided / pause / stop. Support wanted: explanation / reading aloud / language assistance / device assistance / none selected. Fallback: another route / remain undecided / pause / stop.” Leave any item blank. No explanation is required.

Card D — Changed condition. “Imagine staff are temporarily unavailable during this fictional visit. Your preferred route can stay the same while assistance is unresolved. Keep, change, wait without a promised duration, leave undecided, pause or stop. No alternative becomes available because you select it.”

Card E — Current plan and correction. Repeat Card C’s choices for the current plan. “You control continuing. The service owner controls the event requirement. Assistance providers control offered support. Fictional plan; no registration or request sent.” Identify whether a correction changes the initial or current plan. Replace a mark or ask for a restatement; a reason is unnecessary. An unrecorded initial plan stays unrecorded.

Card F — Handling and facilitation. “Before marking, agree how cards will be handled. Folding or covering conceals them; it does not erase them. Leave cards unmarked if preferred.” Facilitator script: “Would you like to point, speak, mark, pass or stop? Shall I read the notice? Which route, if any? Would you like the imagined change? Shall I restate your choice so you can correct it?” Wait for an explicit response; do not select an answer, promise assistance, collect personal information or infer understanding. Facilitation requires an actually available person.

Optional practice card — “Neighborhood Story Circle is invented. Its notice says ‘Check joining arrangements.’ Choose a route and next action using Cards B and C. Imagine your shared-computer time ends. Keep, change, pause or stop. Review using Card E.” Further explanation is available on request, without penalty. This exercise establishes no learning or transfer.

## Acceptance checks

Intended quality is a manageable, correctable decision that preserves participation authority and makes dependencies understandable. Requirements R1–R7 specify proposed observable checks; none has been performed. Intended quality must remain separate from observed technical behavior, which is currently absent.

Technical verification should inspect all reachable states for keyboard focus, text alternatives, reflow, cancellation, complete concealment, faithful summaries and confirmed clearing. It must also verify absence of network, storage, telemetry, personal fields and external navigation.

Affected-person and practitioner review must separately examine whether the task is wanted, whether refusal feels legitimate, which explanations are misunderstood and who bears reading or facilitation work. Do not treat speed, completion, a route change or reduced prompting as evidence of learning, transfer or flourishing.

## Evidence and unknowns

Sequence 2 is preserved context, not a reported interruption or newly verified finding. Sequence 5 is a domain draft; sequence 7 is a systems draft. Neither supplies human approval or executed checks. Field evidence remains pending.

What changes after the hypothetical unavailable-staff challenge: the assistance dependency becomes unresolved while the preference remains under patron control. This contribution additionally makes the initial snapshot optional, keeps critical conditions visible in collapsed views and preserves help during less-prompted practice. These refine current Design; no earlier artifact revision is requested.

Rival explanations for difficulty include unfamiliar wording, language mismatch, inaccessible controls, unnecessary service requirements, limited device time and missing assistance. Apparent ease could reflect prior familiarity or facilitator steering. Unknowns include demand for the exercise, real route availability, paper acceptance, language arrangements, discoverable privacy controls and sustainable support workload.

Agency, dignity, access, belonging and workload require review of actual participation conditions. Learning and transfer require separate inquiry with support and prior familiarity documented. No outcome in these dimensions has been observed.

## Next decision

Prepare a compact screen outline and the complete paper packet for pending patron, librarian and accessibility-practitioner review. ## Problem and people

Learning scientist expert draft for Design deliberation in a rehearsal. No participant observations, practitioner approval, executed checks or learning results exist. Sequence 2 is a preservation event containing earlier Understand, Map and Design context, not a newly verified interaction finding. Sequences 5, 7 and 9 supply the current domain, systems and design drafts.

The fictional task is to explore Community Drawing Hour, inspect its authored confirmation requirement and choose an acceptable next step. Adult patrons with varied reading, language and device access, librarians, volunteers and service owners have relevant interests; none participate here.

The learning question is whether practice could help someone notice a participation condition, distinguish their preference from provision and reconsider a next step. That is a hypothesis. Independent online completion is not the objective. Paper, conditional assistance, an unresolved choice and stopping can all be legitimate outcomes.

## Human and system capability

Human requirements: patrons control participation and can express a decision by selection, pointing or speech. They need not explain a choice or demonstrate understanding to receive the fictional materials. An actually available facilitator may read a notice or restate a selection with permission, but must not choose an answer, treat silence as agreement or promise service assistance.

Librarians and service owners must examine whether the task addresses a wanted problem, whether its service conditions are accurate for any future use, and whether facilitation is feasible. Patron and practitioner review must examine comprehension, language arrangements and the acceptability of practice. These gates remain pending.

System requirements: show the authored requirement, the consequence of an explicit choice and the unresolved dependency beside the decision. Generate no capability label, score, preferred answer or assertion of understanding. Preserve the fixed-choice, no-personal-information design. Keep support preferences distinct from available assistance and retain correction, passing, paper and stopping throughout.

The patron controls whether to continue. The service owner controls participation requirements; assistance providers control support offered. A practice interface cannot supply these missing conditions or establish competence.

## Experience and decisions

Keep the primary task short, as proposed at sequence 9. Selecting a route reveals its consequence without automatically advancing. For example, staff explanation yields: “Your draft seeks an explanation. In this example, an explanation depends on assistance being available. Real availability and language support are unknown. No request is sent.” This describes a choice, not its quality.

The mock online route reveals the invented account requirement without offering account or credential fields. Its meaningful decision is whether to inspect the requirement, seek an explanation if support exists, reconsider another route, leave the action unresolved or stop. There is no correct route imposed by the tool.

Recording an initial plan remains optional under sequence 7. An unrecorded initial plan must stay visibly unrecorded. The patron can inspect the authored unavailable-staff change without recording a baseline. When that change is applied, the staff preference persists while its dependency becomes unresolved. The system does not substitute paper or online practice.

Offer an optional prompt beside the consequence: “Keep this choice, change it, leave it undecided or stop.” Do not ask why. If the patron changes from staff explanation to paper practice, feedback says: “Your current route changed from staff explanation to paper practice. These practice materials are available here; real acceptance of paper remains unknown.” If the patron keeps the preference, say that it remains selected and assistance remains unresolved. Neither response receives praise or a progress judgment.

Review presents a correctable initial/current plan: route, next action, support preference, control boundary and fallback. Generated wording must remain attributable to explicit selections. “None selected” must not become “No support needed.” A patron can reject the wording or choose an unlisted action without entering text.

Neighborhood Story Circle remains optional immediate practice. Its invented notice says “Check joining arrangements”; its changed condition is that shared-computer time ends. Offer fewer initial suggestions while keeping Help, paper, passing and correction equally reachable. Do not reuse the Drawing Hour account requirement as though it were stated in the Story Circle notice. Unknown joining arrangements remain unknown. Task replacement requires an explicit choice and cancellation, as proposed at sequences 7 and 9.

## Requirements and rationale

L1 — Preserve a meaningful decision. Origin: Learning scientist, D2.practice; route conditions at sequence 5 and low-burden interaction at sequence 9. Selecting a route must reveal a concrete authored consequence and leave reconsideration under patron control. The human reason is that practice requires a decision whose implications can be inspected; the system reason is to avoid turning selections into a prescribed sequence. Acceptance check: select staff explanation, apply fictional unavailability, then keep, change or leave the action undecided. Each action must produce a faithful description without automatically selecting a substitute or requiring an explanation. Context: the unavailable-staff condition is hypothetical, not a reported incident.

L2 — Use descriptive, correctable feedback. Origin: Learning scientist, D2.practice; correction rules at sequence 7 and participation authority at sequence 9. Describe what changed and which dependency remains. Do not call a route safe, successful, ready or competent. Acceptance check: record staff explanation, change the current route to paper, correct the initial route to undecided, and cancel a further edit. Both plans and feedback must represent those explicit states; no obsolete staff-derived claim or judgment may remain. Human review must separately establish whether the wording is understandable. A technically faithful summary does not establish that the patron understands it.

L3 — Separate practice from demonstrated transfer. Origin: Learning scientist, D4.transfer; optional second situation at sequences 5, 7 and 9, and the parent learning boundary preserved at sequence 2. Label Story Circle as optional practice, not a transfer test. Give it its own notice and device-time condition; offer help on request without penalty. Acceptance check: enter practice, request detail, leave joining arrangements unresolved, revise or stop. No reward, independence label, competence claim or unlocked service appears. The second task must not invent an account requirement. Context: similar route controls and immediate timing may allow interface familiarity to explain performance.

L4 — Keep any later retention inquiry separate. Origin: Learning scientist, D4.transfer; sequence 2 preserves the requirement for a different task and documented support conditions. The candidate must not retain a learning history, schedule follow-up or infer retention from the initial/current comparison. If humans later authorize an inquiry, use a different fictional notice after a review-selected interval and document the conditions of performance: available information, requested and supplied assistance, prior familiarity and interruptions. Acceptance check for this candidate: every output and Help statement distinguishes immediate supported practice from untested later retention and adaptation. Any future inquiry protocol must be reviewed before use; no interval, recruitment or authorization is established here.

L5 — Preserve a complete non-AI practice route. Origin: Learning scientist, D2.practice and D4.transfer; complete packets at sequences 5, 7 and 9. Keep the same notice, condition, choices, correction and refusal available on paper before digital participation. Pointing or speaking is sufficient if an appropriate person is actually available. Acceptance check: a reviewer can conduct the fictional decision using only the packet below, without digital instructions, personal details or a supplied preferred answer. Printing, language access, handling and facilitator workload remain unknown.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

Descriptive feedback can support reconsideration but also supply reasoning the patron has not independently produced. Keep wording tied to explicit selections and do not treat accepting the summary as understanding. Fewer suggestions may expose a different support need, but may also increase reading and memory demands; Help must remain available.

Retain dissent that a learning exercise may be unnecessary. Improving the event notice, verifying route information or removing a needless account step could address the service barrier directly. Ordinary conversation with available staff and the following paper packet are non-AI alternatives. Review may favor an alternative or stopping development.

Complete invented paper practice packet:

Card A — Mission and notice. “Community Drawing Hour is invented. Its notice offers morning or afternoon sessions and says ‘Confirm your place.’ Choose a possible next step; this does not register anyone. Use no personal information. Point, speak, mark, pass, pause or stop.”

Card B — Routes and conditions. “Online practice: inspect an invented account requirement; create no account and provide no details. Staff explanation: seek an explanation if suitable assistance exists; real availability and language support are unknown. Paper practice: use these cards; real paper acceptance is unknown. No workable route and undecided are legitimate choices.”

Card C — Optional initial plan. “Route: online / staff explanation / paper practice / no workable route / undecided. Next action: inspect requirement / seek explanation if support exists / examine another route / wait without a promised time / action not listed / undecided / pause / stop. Support preference: explanation / reading aloud / language assistance / device assistance / none selected. Fallback: another route / undecided / pause / stop.” Leave any item blank. No reason is required.

Card D — Changed condition. “Imagine staff are temporarily unavailable during this fictional visit. Keep your preference unresolved, change route, wait without a promised duration, leave undecided, pause or stop. Selecting help does not make it available.”

Card E — Current plan and correction. Repeat Card C for the current plan. “You control continuing. The service owner controls the requirement. Assistance providers control support offered. Fictional plan; no registration or request sent.” Correct either plan by replacing a mark or requesting a restatement. An unrecorded initial plan remains unrecorded. No answer is scored.

Card F — Optional practice and facilitation. “Neighborhood Story Circle is invented. Its notice says ‘Check joining arrangements.’ Those arrangements are unresolved. Choose a possible route and next action using Card C. Imagine shared-computer time ends. Keep, change, pause or stop; review using Card E.” Facilitator script: “Would you like the notice read aloud? Which route, if any? Would you like more detail? Keep or change your choice? Shall I restate it so you can correct it?” Ask permission, accept passing and supply no preferred answer. Before marking cards, agree how they will be handled. Covering conceals paper but does not erase it. This practice establishes no learning or transfer.

## Acceptance checks

L1–L5 are proposed checks, not completed tests. Intended quality is a voluntary, inspectable and correctable decision with clear support boundaries. Technical verification may establish that descriptions match selections, corrections remove stale content and optional practice preserves help. It cannot establish comprehension or learning.

Pending human interaction review must examine whether people can recognize what remains unresolved, whether feedback represents their choice, and whether assistance or reading burden is acceptable. Refusal is valid participation, not a failed task. Preserve contrary interpretations and requested corrections.

Learning, retention and transfer require separate reviewed task evidence. Completion, speed, a changed plan, fewer clicks or fewer prompts are insufficient. Agency, dignity, access, belonging and sustainable workload also require evidence about actual participation conditions; none has been observed.

## Evidence and unknowns

Actual earlier references are sequence 2's preserved context and the drafts at sequences 5, 7 and 9. Embedded historical labels in sequence 2 are not additional event evidence. No human approval or field result is supplied.

After the hypothetical unavailable-staff challenge, feedback must expose the unresolved assistance dependency while preserving patron preference. This contribution adds a learning boundary: revising that preference is inspectable behavior, not evidence of improved capability. Story Circle also retains unknown joining arrangements rather than inheriting the account condition from Drawing Hour.

Rival explanations for apparent ease include prior service familiarity, visible suggestions, repeated controls and facilitator prompting. Difficulty could reflect ambiguous wording, language mismatch, inaccessible controls, interrupted device time or unavailable assistance. Unknowns include whether the exercise is wanted, whether its representations are understood, what support is sustainable, and whether any later adaptation occurs. Field evidence remains pending.

## Next decision

Refine the current Design with L1–L5 and prepare the screen outline and paper packet for pending patron, librarian and practitioner review. Examine the value and burden of practice before planning a learning inquiry. Retain dissent, correction and the possibility of a non-AI service improvement. No earlier artifact revision, human approval, pilot authorization or competence claim is requested or supplied.

Expert draft for public deliberation in a rehearsal. No patron, librarian or practitioner has reviewed or approved it. Sequence 2 preserves the parent Understand, Map and Design artifacts as background, including their unresolved human gates and shared-device privacy requirements. Historical sequence labels inside that preserved material are not new evidence for this contribution.

The proposed task is to explore an invented community event, inspect an authored participation requirement and choose an acceptable next step. The people whose interests require review are adult patrons with varied reading, language and device access; librarians and volunteers who may provide assistance; and service owners who control actual event routes. None participate in this demonstration.

D1.problem challenge: difficulty with an account step may reflect an avoidable service requirement, unclear notice or unavailable route. The product must not treat independent online progress as the problem to solve. D5.context challenge: choosing help does not create staff capacity, language assistance, connectivity or time on a shared computer.

## Human and system capability

Human requirements: patrons control whether to continue and may respond by selecting, pointing or speaking. Passing and declining require no justification. Librarians define what assistance can reasonably cover; service owners verify real routes before any later service use. Patron and practitioner review must examine whether the proposed task is wanted and understandable.

System requirements: keep preference separate from provision. For this rehearsal, show authored example conditions alongside each route and retain a visible statement that real availability is unknown. Choosing staff help changes the draft support request, not the staff availability state. Choosing paper opens complete invented materials, not a claim that the real service accepts paper.

Authority remains external to the candidate: it cannot register, reserve help, establish eligibility, verify accounts or determine capability. The candidate should use no open-text fields for this task; fixed choices can express its core decisions without inviting personal information.

## Experience and decisions

Opening mission: “Community Drawing Hour is invented. Explore its example notice and decide what you would do next. This exercise cannot register anyone. Use only the fictional choices shown.” The small route board has text labels for Explore, Choose a route, Check a condition and Review your plan. Illustrations must carry no information absent from those labels.

Invented notice: “Community Drawing Hour offers a morning session and an afternoon session. Materials are provided in this example. The notice says: ‘Confirm your place.’ The route details below are invented for practice.” Session preference is optional and is not a booking.

Offer a local mock online route, asking staff to explain a step, a complete paper practice route, and pause/decline. Include “No route works for me” and “Leave undecided.” Reveal route details when selected. The online detail says: “This example portal requires an account step before confirmation. No account is created here.” Its controls are Inspect the requirement, Seek an explanation, Change route and Stop; it has no account, credential or contact fields.

The staff route says: “You would ask someone to explain the confirmation step. Real assistance and language support are unknown. No request is sent.” The paper route opens the packet below and says: “These are complete practice materials. Real paper acceptance is unknown.”

Record an initial draft using fixed choices. Invite, without requiring, one authored change: “Imagine staff are temporarily unavailable during this fictional visit.” If staff help was selected, retain that preference and visibly mark the dependency as unresolved. Offer wait without a promised time, inspect another route, remain undecided or stop. Never silently substitute an online route.

The final descriptive plan shows Before and Now: chosen route, explicit next action, who controls the relevant condition, support needed and fallback. Use “Not chosen” where a field is undecided. Every entry can be corrected; changing an entry replaces its dependent description. The result always says “Fictional plan; no registration or request sent.” No completion rating or ability judgment appears.

## Requirements and rationale

R1 — Origin: Public library access domain specialist, D1.problem; preserved dependency framing in sequence 2. Pair each route preference with its example condition and unresolved real provision. This prevents an interface choice from implying an available opportunity. Check by selecting staff help and applying the unavailable-staff condition: the preference remains, no assistance is confirmed, and reconsideration is possible without a deficit label.

R2 — Origin: Public library access domain specialist, D1.problem and D5.context; the seed’s unfamiliar-account condition. Keep the mock account step entirely descriptive and provide route reconsideration immediately. This lets a patron inspect a service barrier without disclosing information. Check every screen and state for absence of personal-data fields, account creation, external navigation and registration claims.

R3 — Origin: Public library access domain specialist, D5.context; sequence 2 preserves unknown language arrangements and assistance boundaries. Show “Language support: unknown” near the support decision. Use reviewed plain-language wording and text alternatives; do not invent available translations or interpreters. Permit oral or pointed responses during facilitated practice if a facilitator is actually available. Check that missing language support can leave the plan unresolved or stopped, without blocking access to paper materials. Patron review must determine appropriate language versions; plain English alone does not establish language access.

R4 — Origin: Public library access domain specialist, D5.context; sequence 2 preserves complete concealment, neutral focus and explicit clearing boundaries. Put Cover, Clear and Stop before task controls in keyboard order. Cover hides all route choices, descriptions and change messages from visual and assistive-technology access. Reveal and Resume are distinct actions. Clear removes the candidate-held draft and derived content, confirms that scope, and does not restart a paused or stopped exercise. Check these transitions from every task state, including clearing while covered. Inspect focus placement and magnified reflow. Device-wide removal must never be promised.

R5 — Origin: Public library access domain specialist, D1.problem and D5.context; sequence 2 preserves paper comparison and meaningful refusal. Make the packet below available without completing the digital journey. A patron can point, speak, mark, pass or stop. Check that the packet contains the task, requirement, change, correction and review prompts, and makes sense without interface instructions. Librarian review must examine printing, handling and facilitation effort.

R6 — Origin: Public library access domain specialist, D1.problem; the seed requests a second optional situation. Offer “Neighborhood Story Circle,” an invented event whose notice says “Check joining arrangements.” Present the same route choices with fewer suggestions, while retaining privacy, help, passing and correction. Any additional prompting must be recorded in later reviewed task evidence. Check that practice is optional and unlocks nothing; a changed plan cannot be presented as demonstrated transfer.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

The changed-condition design makes service dependency visible, but may add reading burden. Keep its initial wording short and reveal explanations on request. A complete paper route adds preparation and handling work, but provides a concrete non-AI comparison.

Retain the objection that clearer notices could solve the underlying problem more directly. Alternatives include the paper packet, conversation with available staff and revising service information before building a tool. Reviewers may prefer an alternative or reject the candidate.

Complete invented paper/facilitation packet:

Card A — Task and notice. “Community Drawing Hour is fictional. Choose a possible next step; you are not registering. Morning or afternoon sessions are offered in this example. Its notice says ‘Confirm your place.’ Pass, pause or stop at any time.”

Card B — Routes and conditions. “Online practice: the invented portal includes an account step; do not supply account information. Staff explanation: someone would explain the step if assistance were available; real availability and language support are unknown. Paper practice: use these cards; real acceptance of paper is unknown. You may also choose no workable route or remain undecided.”

Card C — Before plan. “Route: online / staff explanation / paper practice / no workable route / undecided. Next action: inspect the requirement / seek an explanation if support exists / examine another route / pause / stop / undecided. Support wanted: explanation / reading aloud / language assistance / device assistance / none chosen. These choices describe a fictional preference, not available provision.” Marking is optional; pointing or speaking is sufficient.

Card D — Changed condition. “Imagine staff are temporarily unavailable during this fictional visit. Keep your preference, change it, leave it unresolved or stop. Waiting has no promised duration. No route becomes available merely because you choose it.”

Card E — Now plan and correction. Repeat Card C’s choices. Add “Control boundary: service owner controls the event requirement; library staff control assistance offered; you control whether to continue. Fallback: inspect another route / wait without a promised time / leave undecided / stop.” Correct by replacing a selection or asking the facilitator to restate it. Do not require a reason.

Card F — Privacy and facilitation. “Use fictional choices only. Folding or covering cards conceals them; it does not erase them. Agree how marked cards will be handled before practice. Stop or pass without explanation.” Facilitator script: “Would you like to point, speak, mark, pass or stop? What route, if any, would you choose? Here is the imagined change. Keep or change your choice? Shall I read your current plan so you can correct it?” Do not supply an answer, promise assistance or infer understanding. Facilitator availability itself remains a condition to establish.

Optional second card — “Neighborhood Story Circle is fictional. Its notice says ‘Check joining arrangements.’ Choose a route and a next action using Card C. Imagine your shared-computer time ends. ## Acceptance checks

Intended quality: an understandable, correctable route decision that preserves patron control and exposes service dependencies. Proposed checks in R1–R6 cover interaction behavior, privacy, language uncertainty and equivalent alternatives. None has been executed.

Technical verification must separately inspect keyboard order, visible focus, reflow, concealment, stale summaries, confirmed clearing and absence of network, storage and telemetry. Human interaction review must examine whether labels imply real provision, whether stopping is socially acceptable, and what assistance or reading burden the journey creates.

Review flourishing without equating task completion with success: agency includes refusal; dignity excludes deficit labels; access depends on actual conditions; belonging includes usable language arrangements; sustainable workload includes facilitation demand. Learning and transfer require separately reviewed evidence from a different task with support conditions documented.

## Evidence and unknowns

Sequence 2 is preserved parent context, not a participant observation or a technical finding. The seed supplies the fictional mission and restrictions. All requirements here are expert draft proposals. The unavailable-staff change is hypothetical, not a reported event.

Rival explanations for difficulty include ambiguous wording, language mismatch, inaccessible controls, interrupted device time and absent support. Apparent ease could reflect prior familiarity or facilitator prompting. Unknowns include demand for the tool, actual route options, staffing windows, language arrangements, paper acceptance, shared-device behavior and acceptable workload. Field evidence remains pending.

## Next decision

Prepare a candidate Design outline and this complete paper packet for accountable librarian, patron and accessibility-practitioner review. ## Experience and decisions

Keep the primary journey short: explore the invented notice, choose a route, inspect one condition and review a draft. Use the four text-labelled route choices proposed in the seed: mock online practice, staff explanation, complete paper practice, and pause/decline. Also permit no workable route and undecided without requiring an explanation. Use fixed controls and no open-text fields for this candidate.

The first review describes the current choice. An optional explicit action, “Keep this as my initial plan,” records a temporary comparison snapshot. Without that action, show “Initial plan not recorded”; do not fabricate a baseline. Invite the authored change, “Imagine staff are temporarily unavailable during this fictional visit.” Keep the patron's preference and display its unresolved dependency. Offer reconsideration, waiting without a promised duration, remaining undecided or stopping. Never select another route automatically.

The current plan describes route, next action, control boundary, requested support and fallback. It always states “Fictional plan; no registration or request sent.” Changed fields receive descriptive feedback, such as “You changed from staff explanation to paper practice. Real paper acceptance is unknown.” Feedback must derive from explicit choices rather than judge progress.

The optional Neighborhood Story Circle task uses fewer suggestions and its own authored notice. Entering it requires a clear choice to replace the current task, with an opportunity to cancel. It unlocks nothing. Any apparent independence remains uninterpreted until reviewed evidence documents prior familiarity and support.

## Requirements and rationale

R1 — Dependency honesty. Origin: Systems engineer, D1.coupling; domain specialist at sequence 5; preserved Map dependency separation in sequence 2. Selecting a route must reveal its authored requirement, the party controlling it, real provision marked unknown and an action the patron can choose. Selecting staff explanation must leave staff availability unchanged. Acceptance check: select staff explanation, apply fictional unavailability and inspect the plan; the preference remains visible, the dependency becomes unresolved, no help is confirmed and every other route or refusal remains selectable. Context boundary: the changed condition is hypothetical and actual staffing is unknown.

R2 — Correctable comparison. Origin: Systems engineer, D4.verification; before/after proposal at sequence 5; sequence 2's temporary-memory and correction boundaries. Retain at most an explicitly recorded initial snapshot and the current draft within the active session. Generate descriptions from those selections; do not maintain an accumulating choice log. “Correct initial plan” must be distinct from “Change current plan,” with plain labels explaining which side changes. Acceptance check: record an initial staff preference, change the current route to paper, then correct the initial route to undecided. The comparison must describe those exact states and remove obsolete staff-derived claims. A cleared snapshot must never be reconstructed. Context boundary: before/after comparison is a design intention, not measured reflection or learning.

R3 — Separate privacy, activity and content. Origin: Systems engineer, D1.coupling and D4.verification; domain privacy requirement at sequence 5; preserved focus and concealment requirements in sequence 2. Place Cover, Clear and Stop before task controls in keyboard order. Cover hides every choice-bearing view, including both snapshots, feedback, optional practice and assistance descriptions, from visual, keyboard and assistive-technology access. Focus moves to a neutral status. Reveal changes visibility only. Resume is an explicit separate action when activity is paused. Clear remains available while covered or stopped and removes all candidate-held selections and derived task content before confirming its limited scope. It preserves pause or stop and does not create a new draft. Acceptance check: exercise these transitions from an initial/current comparison, a changed-condition view and optional practice; verify neutral focus, no exposed choices while covered, no stale descriptions after clearing and no automatic restart. Context boundary: clearing the candidate does not establish removal of browser, operating-system or device records.

R4 — Recovery without inferred intent. Origin: Systems engineer, D4.verification; sequence 2's interruption and loss boundaries; sequence 5's meaningful refusal. A fictional interruption pauses activity without changing route preference. Cancel closes a pending route change, task replacement or clear confirmation without modifying choices. If the page is reloaded, temporary task state is lost: the opening explains that no prior draft is restored and offers a fresh undecided task, paper materials or stopping. Acceptance check: cancel each pending action, interrupt a changed plan, then reload; unchanged choices survive cancellation, interruption does not silently resume, and reload restores no selections. Context boundary: no persistent storage or recovery history is permitted; these checks have not been executed.

R5 — Equivalent non-AI task and feasible support. Origin: Systems engineer, D1.problem and D1.coupling; domain packet at sequence 5; paper comparison and workload concerns preserved in sequence 2. Make the complete paper packet available before any digital choice. The packet must carry the same authored requirement, changed condition, initial/current choices, control boundary, correction and refusal. Oral assistance is conditional on an actually available person. Acceptance check: a reviewer can conduct the fictional decision using only the packet, without opening the digital route or supplying personal information; the facilitator can restate a corrected choice without selecting an answer. Context boundary: printing, physical access, language arrangements and handling effort need practitioner and affected-person review.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

The initial/current comparison makes a changed decision inspectable but adds state and wording. Keep it optional, retain only two temporary snapshots and show expanded explanations on request. Correctability matters more than filling every field.

Preserve dissent that a planning tool may be unnecessary. A clearer notice, verified route information or removal of a needless account step could address the barrier at its source. Complete paper practice and an ordinary conversation with available staff are non-AI options. None establishes operational service access.

Intended quality is an understandable, correctable decision with visible dependencies and legitimate refusal. R1–R5 define proposed behavioral checks. No check has been run and there is no observed implementation behavior.
